narrative:
The model estimated a 59% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that prediction leaned toward failure, your application was denied: the review treated you as more likely to struggle on the first bar attempt than to pass it.

The largest reason was your third-year class standing. You were in the second decile, well below the average near the sixth decile for accepted students, and this was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.60, above the accepted-student average of about 3.23, was the next most influential factor and worked in your favor, pushing toward a pass. Your LSAT score of 27, substantially below the accepted average of 37.18, was the third-ranked factor and also pushed toward failure.

To strengthen a future application, focus first on the bar-risk indicators you can change: prepare intensively and retake the LSAT, seek admissions counseling about whether additional upper-level coursework or graduate work can offset your class standing, and ask the law school for feedback. Gain substantive legal experience and reapply when your LSAT and academic record show a clear upward trajectory.
